Nvidia ($NVDA) shares now up over 4% in after-hours trading Tuesday, at a session high, after interim CEO Colette Kress raised the company’s revenue growth outlook for fiscal 2028 to 75% from 70% on the earnings call, according to Bloomberg. The stock had swung during the call, briefly turning negative before rallying. The results themselves are covered in my earlier post.

Kress said demand is “far exceeding supply” and pointed to both rising demand and more supply behind the higher outlook. She said Vera Rubin has already brought in about $20 billion of revenue, Nvidia remains confident in the 75% target despite new export rules announced Monday, and total CPU revenue should more than double next fiscal year.

On financing, Kress said Nvidia will be “disciplined and selective” in supporting neoclouds and is rigorously evaluating its investments, commitments and guarantees. She said guarantees begin only once a data center is ready to operate, and customers will need to show they have buyers lined up for the capacity.

Kress also said Nvidia is no longer shipping licensed Hopper products to China. Excluding the $2.4 billion of China shipments disclosed in the CFO commentary, third-quarter revenue would still have been about $113.4 billion, above the $112.6 billion buy-side whisper cited by ZeroHedge.

Board Chair Harvey Jones opened the call by saying the board doesn’t intend to reinstate Jensen Huang and would not take questions on his departure or the board’s investigation. The search for a permanent CEO includes internal and external candidates and “will be thorough,” he said.

Nvidia ($NVDA) cleared seems to have cleared the bar in its first report without Jensen Huang. It beat both consensus and the buy-side whisper on revenue, EPS and guidance. While aAn initial 3% pop has faded to 1.3%, a fraction of the roughly 8% move options were pricing, the positive performance shows investors are overall pleased by the results.

Fiscal third quarter, per the release:
▪️ Revenue $115.8B (+103% from a year ago, +20% from last quarter) vs. $109.0B consensus (TipRanks) and a $112.6B buy-side whisper (JPMorgan survey, via ZeroHedge).
▪️ That’s $7.8B (7.3%) above the midpoint of Nvidia’s own guidance, its biggest dollar beat ever, topping last quarter’s $5.2B, and its biggest percentage beat since the fiscal third quarter of 2025.
▪️ Revenue rose a record $19.6B over last quarter, vs. $14.6B and $13.5B the two quarters before.
▪️ Adjusted EPS $2.68 vs. $2.48 consensus and a $2.63 whisper. GAAP EPS of $2.70 includes $1.8B of net gains on equity stakes.
▪️ The key Data Center metric $107.6B (+110%) vs. $101.9B expected (FactSet, via MarketWatch), now 93% of revenue vs. 90% a year ago.
▪️ AI Clouds, Industrial & Enterprise jumped 195% to $47.5B and supplied 53% of the revenue increase from a year ago. Hyperscale rose 71% to $60.1B.
▪️ Edge Computing $8.2B (+42%) vs. $7.5B expected.
▪️ Adjusted gross margin 74.9%, above the top of the 73.5%-74.5% guided range.

Fiscal fourth-quarter guidance:
▪️ Revenue $130B ±3% vs. $124.9B consensus (TipRanks) and a $129.1B whisper.
▪️ Note the quarter has an extra week. Adjusted for that, implied growth over this quarter is about 4%, vs. 20% this quarter.
▪️ Gross margin 71%-72%, down about 3 points as Rubin ramps, with the midpoint below the 72% whisper.
▪️ No China Data Center compute revenue is assumed, even though $2.4B of Hopper products shipped to China this quarter.

Weak spots under the beat:
▪️ Days sales outstanding rose to 64 from 60, with receivables at $81.0B.
▪️ Inventory climbed to $39.7B from $31.6B.
▪️ Supply commitments rose 40% to $390B, and those due next fiscal year more than doubled to $203B. Total commitments hit $518B, up from $366B.
▪️ Operating cash flow of $48.3B trailed net income of $65.3B.

Cash: free cash flow was $43.8B, and Nvidia returned a record $28.1B to shareholders ($22.1B in buybacks, $6.0B in dividends), with $227.3B of authorization left.

For scale: Nvidia’s Data Center revenue equals about half the roughly $209B the four biggest hyperscalers spent on capex last quarter (Amazon $77.3B, Alphabet $51.4B, Microsoft $45.2B, Meta $34.9B).

The take: Demand clearly isn’t the problem. Rubin is the fastest ramp in Nvidia’s history, and the company is pre-buying supply at a record pace. What matters on the call is whether Kress reaffirms 70%-plus revenue growth for next fiscal year, the bar ZeroHedge and Bloomberg Intelligence flagged, and whether Nvidia keeps funding the AI ecosystem. 

Overhanging all of this of course is the CEO search.

St. Louis Fed’s Musalem (2028 voter)  gives the most aggressive guidance from a Fed official yet on how far and fast he sees the Fed needing to go: “several interest rate increases before the spring of 2027,” starting “soon.”

▪ The math: he puts today’s real policy rate “at the lower end of the 1% to 1.5% range” and wants it “solidly between 2% and 2.5%” by spring. That’s a rise of 1 to 1.5 percentage points, and “the nominal policy rate may need to do most of the work.”
▪ The calendar: only three FOMC meetings come before spring (Dec. 8–9, Jan. 26–27 and March 16–17), so “several” hikes means at least one per meeting.
▪ “In my view, current policy is not yet restraining inflation.” He agrees with Chair Warsh’s description of the September hike as “removing a dose of accommodation.”
▪ He’s “not overly concerned” by the recent tightening of financial conditions, which he says was smaller than after Liberation Day or the start of the Middle East conflict. That’s a direct counter to Daly and Bowman, who see tighter conditions as a reason to go slower.
▪ Inflation: October CPI and PPI suggest October PCE inflation “could be 3.8% and 3.2%” for headline and core, with “three-month rates running above six-month rates for every major category.”
▪ Expectations are anchored “because markets expect that the FOMC will raise its policy rate within the next few months.” “Moving sooner, while inflation expectations are anchored, has a better chance of succeeding.”
▪ Like Warsh on Monday, he doesn’t see an AI productivity boom yet: “the economy does not yet appear to be in a high-productivity growth regime.”

That said, it's worth remembering that this isn’t the first time Musalem has staked out a very hawkish position. In June 2024 he said rate cuts could take “months, and more likely quarters.” Eight weeks later, he said “the time may be nearing” for one, and the Fed cut by half a point in September.

In that respect in a statement that seems hard to square he said he somehow also sees “an unlikely but still plausible scenario in which additional policy firming will not be required.” That could happen if energy and shipping costs fall, productivity picks up, or AI spending or wealth-driven consumer spending slows.

He joins Logan, Hammack, and Waller in calling for a faster pace but importantly doesn't have a vote until 2028.  All 13 officials who’ve spoken on rates since the Nov. 5 selloff lean toward more hikes.

The Atlanta Fed’s Q4 real GDP tracker though eased to +3.38%, the least since its +3.22% initiation on October 29th, down from +3.48% on November 9th.

The biggest move since the last update was a -0.15% drop in the contribution from residential investment (to -0.12% from +0.03%), mostly after last Wednesday’s existing home sales report. 

Consumption's contribution also fell -0.07% (to +1.72% from +1.79%), mostly after today’s reports (which looks strange given the strength of the control group, but the model actually raised its goods spending estimate; the drag came from services, led by a plunge in October utility spending in today’s industrial production data and a drop in restaurant sales; also September retail spending was revised up giving a higher compare). Those were partly offset by gains in inventories (+0.09%) and government spending (+0.06%).

As a reminder, the Atlanta Fed’s tracker started very strong in each of Q1, Q2 and Q3 before falling sharply as we approached the actual GDP reads: Q1 went from 3.13% to 1.99%, Q2 from 3.70% to 1.50%, and Q3 from 4.95% to 3.37%. @C_Barraud’s Tuesday Morning Brief had a couple of posts on the recent troubles of Leopold Aschenbrenner’s Situational Awareness. The fund’s third-quarter 13F, filed yesterday, holds an important lesson for investors. Its thesis (bets on AI) didn’t sink it. The fund returned 439% through June on that thesis. What sank it was a capital structure that couldn’t survive a drawdown.

▪️ July was the real blowup, and leverage caused it. The fund reportedly ran about 4x leverage. At 4x, a 25% drop in your holdings wipes out 100% of your capital, and AI infrastructure stocks have fallen that much several times in this cycle. When they fell in July, the losses reportedly triggered margin calls, and the fund sold its entire stock book to Citadel. Its investor letter showed a 67% loss for the month, and Bloomberg put assets at about $10B afterward, down from about $45B at the start of July. Recovery math is brutal: a 67% loss needs a 203% gain just to break even.

▪️ The downside protection came off at the wrong time. As of March 31, the fund reported puts covering $8.5B of stock in Nvidia ($NVDA), Broadcom ($AVGO), Oracle ($ORCL), Advanced Micro Devices ($AMD) and a VanEck ETF. By June 30, those puts were down to $5M, just before the July selloff.

▪️ Adding to the damage was a separate bet against software. The fund was also reportedly short software stocks, and those rose in July while its AI holdings fell, so even the short bets lost money.

▪️ The rebuild was a more defined-risk bet, but it looks badly timed. As of September 30, two-thirds of the $1.58B public book (down 92% from $20.2B at June 30) was call options on Bloom Energy ($BE), Nebius ($NBIS), Sandisk ($SNDK) and a memory chip ETF. Through Monday those stocks are down 35% to 55% from quarter-end, and the fund’s biggest stock position, SharonAI ($SHAZ), is down 63%.

Note, though, this isn’t a second blowup despite headlines. The public book is a small slice of a roughly $10B fund that’s mostly private holdings, led by an Anthropic stake Bloomberg valued at about $5B. At Monday’s prices, the stock positions are down about $325M, a few percent of the fund. The calls can lose at most what was paid for them, which the filing doesn’t disclose. Unlike borrowed money, they can’t force a fire sale.

The takeaway isn’t to avoid leverage or options. The same 4x leverage produced the 439%. The takeaway is to size positions so a normal drawdown can’t force you out. Losing money you’ve set aside to put at risk is survivable. Being forced to sell at the bottom is what turns a drawdown into a permanent loss

Nvidia ($NVDA) is one down week away from tying its longest weekly losing streak on record.

▪ Six straight down weeks through Friday cut the stock 30.4% from its October 2 close. Monday’s 4.1% drop to $156.14 has week seven started.

▪ The only other seven-week run since the 1999 IPO was June 6 to July 18, 2008, when NVDA fell 53.2%. It has never fallen eight weeks in a row.

▪ Six-week runs are slightly less rare: one in 2002 and two in 2012. 

▪ At −33.3% so far, it’s also the fourth-deepest of the 13 streaks of 5+ weeks, behind May–June 2002 (−56.1%), 2008 (−53.2%) and March–April 2002 (−37.1%).

▪ The stock is now about 35% ($2 trillion in market cap per the WSJ) below its October 6 record close of $239.24.

What NVDA did after the 12 prior streaks of 5+ weeks (measured from the last down week’s close):

▪ 4 weeks later: higher just 5 of 12 times, median −1.4%.

▪ 13 weeks later: also higher 5 of 12 times, median −6.3%.

▪ 52 weeks later: higher 9 of 12 times, median +30.4%.

And the deep streaks (30%+ declines) were lower 13 weeks later in 4 of 5 cases, including −34% after 2008 and −46% and −50% after the two 2002 runs. One for the bulls: the last streak, which ended in October 2022, was followed by a 305% gain over the next year as the AI trade took off.

So the end of a long losing streak hasn’t been much of a buy signal for NVDA. A payoff might come on a one-year view, and that depends on the fundamentals holding up.

Ahead of Nvidia ($NVDA) earnings Tuesday, the Commerce Department moved Monday on the China loophole J.P. Morgan’s Michael Cembalest flagged in Friday’s Eye on the Market (“The Icarus Files”).

The new rule takes effect in 90 days. It requires a license for chips going to overseas data centers that sell significant computing power to Chinese companies, and for advanced chip exports to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.

Why it matters, per Cembalest’s numbers:

▪️ Remote access to US chips is the largest single source of China’s projected AI compute at the end of 2027 (32%), according to the Institute for Progress.
▪️ 75% of China’s overseas compute sits in Southeast Asia.
▪️ The share of Nvidia’s revenue billed to Singapore addresses rose from 8% to 22% after the Biden-era export controls, and Nvidia stopped breaking it out in July 2025.
▪️ The House passed the Remote Access Security Act 369–22, but the Senate never took it up. Cembalest wrote that China hawks “appear to have the upper hand right now in DC.” Three days later, Commerce acted on its own.

His point is that the leadership fight isn’t the main risk; Nvidia’s weakening moat is. Nvidia holds 39% of frontier labs’ future compute deals, down from its 80%+ market share in 2023–2025. One frontier lab now gets models running on AMD chips in three days instead of 6–12 months.

If the remote-access curbs work, Chinese labs have more reason to build their own chips, and https://t.co/n1ZNIXVuhx, DeepSeek and Meituan already train and run models on Huawei’s Ascend.

He still sees a long-term case at a 0.2x PEG and 32% below the high, but it rests on the business, not the CEO.

Nvidia fell 4.1% Monday to become the third-largest US company for the first time in 18 months. It’s now down more than $2T from its October high, per the WSJ. Options price an 8% move on Tuesday’s report.

In US economic data, Tuesday brings us October retail sales, industrial production and import prices, plus September business inventories and the November NAHB housing market index. We’ll also get the weekly ADP report.

Fed speakers include St. Louis Fed President Musalem (2028 voter), Fed Governor Waller, Cleveland Fed President Hammack (2026 voter) and New York Fed President Williams (permanent voter).

Three S&P 500 components report, all with market caps over $100B:

Before the open: Home Depot ($HD) and Disney ($DIS).

After the close: Nvidia ($NVDA).

Outside the S&P 500 we’ll hear from https://t.co/pbxL6tGgRA ($JD) and Viking ($VIK).

Ex-US highlights include the minutes of the RBA’s November meeting, the UK’s September labor market report, Germany’s November ZEW survey, Italy’s final October CPI and the European Commission’s autumn economic forecast. Hungary’s central bank announces a rate decision, ECB chief economist Lane speaks at Harvard along with Cipollone and Moulin, and RBA Governor Bullock joins a panel. 

The APEC CEO Summit gets underway in Shenzhen, and EU defense ministers meet on Ukraine and EU-China relations.

@C_Barraud’s Monday Morning Brief had a few posts on China's monthly economic data that missed across the board. While the consumer was weak, the bigger story was investment falling apart despite Beijing’s stimulus efforts.

The headline misses:
▪️ Retail sales rose just 0.4% from a year earlier (vs. 0.8% expected and 1.1% in September), with autos (−21.4%) the biggest drag, per BofA.
▪️ Industrial output slowed to 4.8% (vs. 5.3% expected), its first slowdown in three months.
▪️ Fixed-asset investment fell 8.1% year to date (vs. −7.0% expected and −7.2% through September).

That −8.1% is the weakest year-to-date reading since the 2020 Covid shutdown (−10.3% through April 2020). It’s also a sharp reversal: investment started 2026 up 1.8% and has slid almost every month since, after falling 3.8% in all of 2025.

By BofA’s calculation, single-month investment fell 16.1% from a year earlier in October, more than double September’s −7.2%, and that’s against an easy comparison (October 2025 was already down by double digits):
▪️ Infrastructure fell 17.6% (from −10.5%), after starting the year up 11.4%.
▪️ Property investment fell 33.2% (from −20.6%).
▪️ Manufacturing investment fell 9.3%.

BofA calls the infrastructure drop “especially disappointing,” given reports that the full RMB800B in policy financing tools had been deployed by the end of October. Its Beijing macro tour found limited support at the local level, and it warns growth could weaken further toward year-end if the current policy mix doesn’t stop the slide.

Nor is the PBOC rushing to help. Another headline in the brief says it withdrew medium-term funds, a warning sign for anyone betting on easing.

The one bright spot: urban unemployment edged down to 5.1% from 5.2%.

For U.S. markets, a weakening China is worth watching as a possible offset to the commodity-driven inflation the Fed is fighting.
